title: Structures and pointers; arrow member access
learningObjectives: Explain the C concept and its rules.
Trace the example and describe data flow.
Identify relevant failure and boundary cases.
Apply the concept in a tested C program.

understand.concept: A pointer to a structure can access a member using the -> operator. The expression pointer->member is equivalent to (*pointer).member. The pointer must designate a live structure object before member access.
understand.whyItMatters: Pointers avoid copying large structures and allow functions to update caller-owned records, but invalid or null pointers must not be dereferenced.
understand.analogy: Treat the operation as a clearly specified contract between the program and its data.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's type, lifetime, I/O and object representation rules.

explain.narrative:
A pointer to a structure can access a member using the -> operator. The expression pointer->member is equivalent to (*pointer).member. The pointer must designate a live structure object before member access.

Check all return values, object lifetimes, types and preconditions. Enable compiler warnings and test expected as well as failure paths.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.explanation: The function receives the address of p. point->x selects the x member of the pointed-to structure and increments it. The output is 4,4.

practise.guidedTask: Rewrite point->x as an equivalent expression using * and dot.
practise.independentTask: Write a function that receives a pointer to a structure and updates two fields after validating the pointer.
hints: The -> operator combines dereferencing and member selection.
A non-null structure pointer may still be dangling or invalid.
Use const struct Type * when the function should only inspect the structure.
